title: The Battle of Gonzales
summary: Decide whether a small skirmish over a cannon — the 'Come and Take It' fight of October 2, 1835 — was truly the turning point that began the Texas Revolution.
challenge: On October 2, 1835, Texian colonists at Gonzales refused to hand a small cannon back to Mexican soldiers and fired on them instead, under a homemade flag reading 'Come and Take It.' Almost no one was hurt — so why do historians call this the turning point that began the Texas Revolution? Map what led up to it and what changed afterward.

event.title: Battle of Gonzales ('Come and Take It')

mapData.before: Anglo colonists and Tejanos lived fairly autonomously in Mexican Texas under the 1824 federal constitution; Gonzales kept a small cannon, loaned in 1831, for defense against raids.
mapData.pressures: Santa Anna shifted Mexico toward centralism, dismantling the 1824 federal system and alarming Texans; Colonel Ugartechea demanded the loaned Gonzales cannon back, and the colonists refused.
mapData.turning: Texian militia crossed the Guadalupe River at dawn and fired on Lt. Castañeda's dragoons rather than surrender the cannon — the first shots of the Texas Revolution.
mapData.immediate: Castañeda withdrew toward San Antonio de Béxar empty-handed; 'Come and Take It' became a rallying cry; volunteers streamed to Gonzales.
mapData.longer: The gathering force marched on Béxar (captured December 1835); delegates convened the Consultation, moving Texas toward the 1836 declaration of independence.
mapData.whoPushed: Gonzales colonists and DeWitt-colony militia (the 'Old Eighteen' and John Henry Moore), determined to keep the cannon.
mapData.whoResisted: Mexican centralist authorities — Colonel Ugartechea and Lt. Castañeda, ordered to recover the cannon.
mapData.couldDiffer: Castañeda was ordered to avoid a fight; had he pressed the attack, or had colonists complied, revolution might have been delayed or sparked elsewhere.
mapData.whyKey: Why do historians call a small skirmish with almost no casualties the 'turning point' that began the Texas Revolution? What changed after Gonzales that could not be undone?

teacherText.keyideas: The Battle of Gonzales (Oct. 2, 1835) was the first military engagement of the Texas Revolution. The dispute centered on a small bronze cannon loaned to the colony in 1831 on condition it be returned. When Mexican authorities demanded it back, colonists raised a 'Come and Take It' flag and fired. Casualties were minimal (about two Mexican soldiers), but the symbolic refusal set the Revolution in motion.
teacherText.misconceptions:
• The battle's importance is symbolic, not military — almost no one was hurt.
• 'Come and Take It' was a colonists' banner, not an official Texas flag at the time.
• The fight did not by itself win independence; it began a chain leading to San Jacinto (1836).
teacherText.vocabulary: Texas Revolution, centralism, Constitution of 1824, militia, dragoons, Consultation, San Antonio de Béxar.
teacherText.context: Cannon delivered to DeWitt's colony March 10, 1831; Col. Ugartechea demanded its return in 1835; Lt. Castañeda led ~100 dragoons; Texian militia under John Henry Moore fired Oct. 2, 1835; Castañeda withdrew to Béxar. Led to the siege of Béxar (Dec. 1835) and the 1836 independence movement.
